newsitem.title: GERMANY: German share funds surge, bull run lures investors.
newsitem.headline: German share funds surge, bull run lures investors.

text.p: Germany's share market is no longer the exclusive preserve of grey-suited Frankfurt bankers, as small investors scramble to put their money in equity funds, eager to join in the DAX index's greatest ever bull run.

"Germans storm the bourse" ran the headline in Germany's mass circulation Bild newspaper on Thursday. While this smacks of hyperbole, figures released on Friday by the German investment fund association BVI back up the headlines.

In the first half of 1997, 15.7 billion marks was placed in German equity funds, compared with 900 million marks a year earlier, bringing total investment in share funds above the one-hundred-billion mark level for the first time.

The blue-chip DAX index has risen around 50 percent since the start of the year and while much of this relates to institutional investors, massive inflows into equity funds have proven pivotal in freeing up investment capital in Germany.

The bull-run is obviously not just a German phenomenon, and investors also seem interested in investing in international equity funds and buying portfolios of shares in other high performance markets in the United States and Asia.
Altogether, inflows into investment funds in the first half of the year amounted to 68.2 billion marks, bringing the total under management to a record level of 962 billion marks.
This divided into 479 billion marks invested in retail funds and 483 billion in special funds.

Of the total put into retail funds, 245.1 billion was invested in bond-backed funds, which are still the strongest component of the investment fund market in Germany. Equity funds accounted for 101.3 billion marks and 78 billion in property funds.
Of the total under management, 47.8 billion marks was focused on German-based equity funds, 40.2 billion in special international funds and 13.3 billion marks in general international funds.
Inflows into bond-backed funds grew five billion marks in the first six months, but current low interest rate environment means that investors are favouring equity-backed funds.

Of the 15.6 billion marks invested in equity funds in the first half, 8.2 billion went into special international share funds, 5.9 billion into general international share funds and 1.6 billion marks into German-based share funds.

Investors are also keeping one eye on the future of pension provision. The traditional pay-as-you-go system still holds sway in Germany, but many pundits say that a rapidly-ageing population means that it is a question of when, and not if, private pension provision will be introduced.

The real engine behind the growth in investment funds was the 20-billion mark Deutsche Telekom IPO in November last year, which has transformed the image of equities and share-backed funds in the German investment arena.
"German investors have grown their awareness of the share market through the flotation of Deutsche Telekom," a BVI spokesman told Reuters.

The increased liquidity of the German market has prompted 12 German companies to list on the bourse so far this year and this has prompted more than 20 other German firms to plan initial public offerings (IPOs).
High profile listings include the German television network ProSieben AG, shares in which jumped 32 percent on their first day of trading last week with a traded volume of 2.7 million shares.
